speakeroldname: Hon. Bryce S. Mackasey (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TRANSITIONAL ASSISTANCE BENEFIT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to
announce changes in the TAB or transitional assistance benefit program. I shall read this four page document as rapidly as possible. The purpose of these amendments is to extend the duration of the TAB program for another 18 months. Hon. members will recall that the program was to have ended on December 31 of this year. In addition there are a number of changes that will make the program of greater assistance to workers laid off in the automotive industry. It will better serve its original purpose, which is to ensure that the auto pact, which benefits the whole economy, is not effected at the expense of workers in the automotive industry.
It is proposed to extend the transitional assistance benefit program by 18 months, as I said, so that a lay-off can be certified as coming under the terms of the program up to June 30, 1970. This, hon. members will note, is the same date as that to which the assistance to firms in the industry under the loan program is being contemplated.
The rules on the eligibility of an individual for TAB will be eased. It is proposed that an employee be eligible if he has worked 16 weeks in the industry in the past 52 weeks. Previously the time required was 30 weeks. He must still be qualified for unemployment insurance.
The formula for benefit has been improved. It is now based on one week of benefit for every two weeks worked in the automotive industry in the past two years. The old formula provided four weeks of benefit to employees who had qualified by working 30 weeks in the previous 52, with one extra week of benefit for each additional week of service in that year, plus one week of benefit for each week of service in the year before the previous 52 weeks.
The 52 week maximum benefit is retained, but with the shorter qualifying period this
change will allow a longer benefit period for employees with short service in the industry. It is proposed that this change be made retroactive to November 22, 1968.
An employee's entitlement to TAB remains in effect until it is exhausted, up to the expiry date of the program. At present that date is December 27, 1969. That is one year beyond the present termination date of the program. As things stand now a worker certified on that date who had a full year of entitlement to supplementary assistance benefit would never have a chance to draw TAB because the supplementary assistance benefit would have to be taken first. Thus he would be discriminated against compared with workers certified early in the program.
It is proposed that all workers be treated alike by assuring a three year period of entitlement regardless of when the lay-off was certified. The final cut-off point for receiving TAB benefit would be June 30, 1973.
At present an employee must use up any supplementary unemployent benefit to which he is entitled before he can draw TAB. It is proposed that an employee be allowed to choose which benefit he draws first, but not to allow both to be drawn at the same time. However, it is expected that in almost every case the employee will elect to draw supplementary unemployment benefit first because that would be in his best financial interest.
To sum up, these amendments will extend the life of the TAB program by a year and a half, will provide more assistance to workers with short service in the automotive industry, and will allow workers to choose which of SUB or TAB they will draw first. The amendments make some other minor modifications of an administrative nature.

I also commend the minister for the changes in the TAB regulations. This is something which had been pressed for by members of this party as is shown in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition and myself as reported at page 3132 of Hansard for November 25, 1968. We certainly go along with the changes. I note that the life of the TAB agreement and regulations will be extended for a year and a half. Another important change is that which gives the option of choosing between SUB and TAB, whichever the worker wishes to take. This is a good move.

I think this should be done. I think of places like Bell Island. My friend the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) represents that area. I think of the Sydney steel situation which is important, particularly to the people of Nova Scotia. I believe special consideration should be given to this. I realize that the minister is waiting for the Woods task force report. We are all waiting anxiously for this report, and hope something

will be done in this regard, to look after the employees.
This measure assists the unemployment situation in the Windsor area. I hope the minister and the government will now come forward with policies to assist the very great number of unemployed throughout this country at this time. We know the latest figures are high. I think of the heavy unemployment in the shipyards, in the fisheries and in the rail car industry in my area, as well as others.

speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Finance and Manpower and Immigration as follows: 1. The federal government cannot in isolation solve the problem of summer employment for students. December 18. 1968

students who have a source of income do not require the same measure of assistance. The government therefore does not plan to bring in legislation to make part time students eligible. Loans, by the terms of the act, are authorized only to students in need of a loan in order to pursue their course of studies. Revised federal-provincial agreed criteria are in effect this year on the basis of which need is determined by the provinces. Indications are that they are effective in ensuring that funds are available to those who really need them, and no change is being contemplated to make it easier to obtain loans to those who do not really need assistance. The house resumed from Tuesday, December 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-146, respecting the imposition of antidumping duty1-Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) for Mr. Benson-Mr. Faulkner in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: DANGER FROM U.S. ANTI-BALLISTIC MISSILES NEAR CANADIAN BORDER
speechtext:
Order. House again in committee of the whole on Bill C-146, an act respecting the imposition of anti-dumping duty. When the committee rose last evening clause 19, with an amendment, was under consideration. I shall reread the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West:
That clause 19(1) be amended by deleting all the words after "the" in line 31 and by adding the words "date of the publication of the decision in the Canada Gazette".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: DANGER FROM U.S. ANTI-BALLISTIC MISSILES NEAR CANADIAN BORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after the house rose yesterday evening I asked the officials of the departments concerned to give very careful consideration to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West, and very careful consideration has been given to it. As I said yesterday evening, it is a question of some difference of opinion, not on ways but on means, since there is no doubt the government wishes to give full opportunity for the lodging of appeals under the provisions of clause 19 to those who are interested in doing so.
However, it should be noted, Mr. Chairman, that in none of the briefs presented to the standing committee nor in any of the briefs presented to the interdepartmental committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Glass was there any complaint made by either importers, exporters or manufacturers, about the time or method of filing notice of appeal under clause 19. In other words, those who would be concerned with the provisions of clause 19 did not appear to foresee the possible difficulties that were foreseen by the hon. member who moved the amendment.
I should also like to draw to the attention of the hon. member that the clause seems to cover appeals from two kinds of decisions of the deputy minister, those under clause 17(1) and those under clause 18(4). I am advised it is only for those decisions under clause 17(1) that there must be publication of the decision in the Canada Gazette. Therefore the method proposed by the hon. member would not, in my respectful opinion and submission, achieve the aim he has in mind.
I might add one or two other points because I want to demonstrate that serious consideration is being and has been given to

the points he has raised. If there continues to be difference of opinion, it is not because of any difference of aims with respect to the wide provision of notice of appeal.
As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, this subclause relates to imports, in other words the individual entry of goods, after an order or finding of a tribunal that there has been injury caused by dumping, and it is considered to be quite different in scope from the "determination" of the deputy minister under clause 17(1). It is at this point in the scheme of legislation that the change is made from looking at the dumping of a series of imports to levying the duty entry by entry, while clause 18(4) relates to the liability for duty on a particular entry after a finding of injury.
The appeal scheme to which I have made reference, from customs appraisers to the deputy minister and then to the Tariff Board, which is proposed here, is a precise parallel to the provisions in the Customs Act. In the committee hearings no one proposed that the deputy minister's determinations on individual entries be made public because generally these provisions are considered by business communities to be of a fair and reasonable nature. It might also be argued that further publicity at this stage, before an importer may decide to appeal to the Tariff Board, might be considered by some as a harassment and deterrent to the use of appeal.
It could also be argued that from the export point of view publicity of this sort might have some inhibition on exports and we would not wish to see this kind of publicity given in our export markets. To conclude, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that we are moving into a complex new area of administration in which procedural questions and rules are vital.

At that time it would be possible to provide an occasion for the discussion of the provisions, if such should be deemed necessary. I would suggest to the hon. member that he may wish to accept this suggestion in lieu of his amendment; otherwise, I regret that I do not have the authority

Since the verb "to dump" does not exist in French, we resort to another word to express the same concept. Since considerable time has passed, some 15 days since he first introduced the resolution, a resolution which is very carefully worded, I believe it would be proper that I put its words on the record. The resolution states:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to regulate interprovincial and export trade in freshwater fish and to establish the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation; to provide that the corporation shall conduct its operations on a selfsustaining financial basis without appropriations therefor by parliament; to provide that the governor in council may authorize the Minister of Finance, under certain terms and conditions, to guarantee repayment of loans by banks to the corporation and to make loans to the corporation, the aggregate outstanding of amounts borrowed or loaned not to exceed five million dollars; to provide also for grants to the corporation, out of the consolidated revenue fund, not exceeding in the aggregate of one hundred thousand dollars to enable the corporation to meet initial operating and establishment expenses; and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.
The dictionary gives one of the meanings of the word expedient as being "more politic than just". I cannot help but wonder if this resolution is more politics than justice, more of a promise than a possibility for the future well being of our inland fishermen. I say this because the list of unfulfilled promises made to our fishermen over the years is quite lengthy. The economic hardships faced by large sections of the fisheries are tragic reminders of the government's attitude toward this important primary industry.
Let us look at some of the promises that have been made by the Liberals in the past. Mr. Chairman, I am not going to read the entire list since it is the wish of many of us to get out of here by Christmas, but I will place a few of their statements pertaining to fisheries on the record.
For example a five day federal-provincial fisheries conference was held in Ottawa on January 20, 21, 22, 23 and 24, 1964, behind closed doors. When it concluded a 1,800 word communique was read by the then minister of fisheries, Mr. Robichaud, to a press conference. It said the future of the Canadian fishing industry is bright if a "progressive program of education, modernization and economic encouragement is adopted." The minister pledged to design a national development program that would bring the Canadian fishermen the same benefits given to Canadian farmers. There were no specific details set out at that time by the minister.

Those dates, Mr. Chairman, were January 20, 21, 22, 23 and 24 in 1964. The minister pledged to design a national development program that would bring Canadian fishermen the same benefits given to Canadian farmers. There were no specific details set out by the minister but his communique did refer to the general agreement reached with the provinces for improved credit facilities for our fishermen, as well as new research programs, exploration programs and technical training. This communique was hailed as a Magna Carta for the fishermen although it was estimated it would take five or more years to get the whole program developed.
I ask the minister who is piloting this resolution through the house this afternoon if this freshwater fish marketing corporation is to be the Magna Carta for our national fishing industry? If it is, then I say to him that it falls painfully short of the promise made by the former minister of fisheries almost five years ago that a national development program for our fishing industry would be established by this government.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, this resolution sets a bad precedent for it implies that only one section of Canada's fisheries, namely our inland fisheries, is facing economic difficulties and therefore requires additional government planning and control. This resolution ignores the problems of salmon fishermen on the west coast. It ignores the problems of our deep sea fishermen who are faced with low prices for their catch and higher production costs. It does nothing for the thousands of fishermen on the Atlantic coast engaged in the salt cod industry, or for the thousands of our inshore fishermen who daily watch the fleets of other nations grow larger and operate in what should be Canada's territorial seas, taking not only their supplies of fish but in some cases destroying their set nets and traps as well.
In my opinion it is pointless to state that you can segregate the problems of the fishing industry. The minister, in his initial statement, said that inland fish do not compete directly with markets enjoyed by ocean fish. I say to this house that the products of the inland fishing industry must compete in the marketplace with all other forms of protein, including salt water fish. It is only natural therefore, since the entire fishing industry is facing severe marketing difficulties, that the

December 18. 1968
Fisheries
freshwater fishing industry would be similarly affected, but the methods proposed to overcome these difficulties cannot help but cause concern within the entire industry.
When considering a fisheries policy for Canada, or for any section of the industry in Canada, I believe the government should be primarily concerned with the individual fishermen and the impact that any new policy will have upon his way of life, upon his income, and upon his standard of living. We must ask ourselves if this policy will rob him of any of his freedoms, if it will improve his income, or advance his training in new and better methods of participation in the fishing industry.
I realize, as well as any one in this house, that the problems of the fishing industry are many and complex, and I cannot help but wonder whether the federal government, in introducing this resolution, is once again overstepping its boundaries of authority by usurping rights which, under the British North America Act, are vested in the provincial governments. I say this because the fisheries minister stated in his first appearance before the standing committee on fisheries and forestry that the provinces have property rights in non-tidal fisheries. He also stated that while all the regulations governing fisheries are made at Ottawa, the enforcement of the regulations, mostly in the freshwater fisheries, have been undertaken by a number of provincial governments concerned, which have also established agencies to promote the development of the fishing industry within their provinces.

Mr. Chairman, as I stated a moment ago to the minister I am unable to verify whether or not we can conclude the
December 18, 1968

debate on this resolution. I believe he understands the reason I am unable to give such an undertaking. However I wish to thank the other members of the committee for having granted permission to continue discussion of the resolution at this time.
Since this resolution proposes to regulate interprovincial and export trade in freshwater fish, one of the first questions that comes to mind is as to whether the federal government obtained agreement with all the provincial governments concerned, before proceeding with this arbitrary legislation which presumes to take over some of the authority now vested in the provincial governments? I believe this question must be answered, in view of the present government's attitude toward existing shared cost programs which eventually will leave the provinces with social care programs which they will have to run and finance by themselves. Will this program operate, as the resolution states, on a self-sustaining financial basis and, if so, how will the individual fisherman benefit from this scheme. It seems to me that at the present time the inland fishermen are overloaded with overhead. Before their catch reaches the consumer, who primarily is in the United States, it must go through the hands of the dealer, the processor, the exporter, the United States importer and, finally, the United States retailer.
With all this overhead is it any wonder that there are no worse pockets of poverty in all Canada than those found in the northern sections of our inland fishery. And now these poor fishermen are to have an additional board which will be supported out of their meagre earnings, because this resolution states that the board is to be self-sustaining. I ask the minister: How do you lighten a man's load by adding to his burden?
Just what is the situation within the freshwater fishing industry in this country? Normally, the supply of freshwater fish in Canada runs between 100 million and 125 million pounds. Its value to an estimated 7,000 fishermen is approximately $8J million with an export value of $13 million. The most important species in terms of income to the fishermen are whitefish, pickerel, sauger, lake trout, pike, perch, smelt and cisco. The importance of this industry is evident when one compares these figures to the over-all total Canadian production which amounts to two and a half billion pounds, valued to the fishermen at $162 million. For some time many of these inland fishermen have been
Fisheries
unable to obtain an income from fishing which would provide them with an adequate standard of living. Some of them have been able to supplement their low income from fishing through taking part time employment, but many freshwater fishermen have no other employment opportunities and consequently are living at subsistence levels. Primarily such conditions exist in northern Ontario, the northern parts of the prairie provinces and the Northwest Territories. In these areas the failure of the freshwater fisheries to support normal living conditions is associated more and more with the Indian and Metis, as more of these people have entered the commercial fisheries in recent years.
The marketing of pike, pickerel, whitefish, sauger and lake trout is of major concern to the 7,000 fishermen, 300 dealers and 35 exporters in the western inland fisheries and in northern Ontario. To add to their problems the incidence of parasite infected whitefish is increasing. This is of concern to everyone, since 70 per cent of the freshwater fish from the Northwest Territories and approximately 50 per cent of the catch in Saskatchewan and Manitoba are whitefish. The presence of the parasite is a major problem to the freshwater fish industry because the United States food and drug administration prohibits the entry of infected whitefish under the food, drug and cosmetics act of 1906. All whitefish entering the United States are therefore subject to inspection and rejected shipments, having suffered considerable deterioration in quality are returned to Canada and are subsequently marketed for a greatly reduced return in the domestic market.
In order to minimize the effect of this action of the Canadian freshwater fishing industry and to determine the amount of infection, the whitefish export inspection regulations were established on March 8, 1951 under the Canadian Fish Inspection Act. Under these regulations inspection is carried out by Canadian inspectors who cut up a number of whitefish from each shipment to determine the incidence of the parasite. However, the fish used as samples are not paid for by the federal government and they represent a loss to the exporters and the fishermen. Unfortunately, even with this Canadian inspection at export points, and their rejection of some 5 per cent of all shipments, a great deal of whitefish continue to be rejected by United States inspectors- something in the order of 15 per cent of all shipments-because the samples used in both

December 18, 1988
Fisheries
countries to determine infection are too small to give consistent results.
It is obvious therefore that there is little ground for confidence on the part of the United States authorities in the methods used byCanadian authorities to determine the rate of infection in whitefish. Since the presence of this parasite and the present system of inspection and re-inspection is without question one of the most important problems affecting any single species in the freshwater fishing industry, I cannot help but wonder why the federal government has not taken action to help solve this problem. Why did not the federal government improve its inspection service at the processing level, where the fish are packed, in the same manner that codfish and saltwater fish are inspected? In this way there would be a greater quality control at the producer level and, since top quality commands top prices in any commodity, part of the freshwater fisherman's problem would be solved.
I would also ask this government why they have not made a formal approach to the United States government requesting them to establish a set of standards for the inspection of whitefish which is mutually satisfactory to both countries. We must know, for example, that a fish which has been graded as "clear" in Canada at the source of production will be accepted as "clear" by the United States food and drug administration inspectors. It seems to me that a set of standards could be adopted which would be universally accepted by both countries and which would help eliminate some of the losses presently borne by the inland fishermen. In fact I submit that this is the course which will have to be followed by the government, regardless of the final method used to market our freshwater fish because quality control at the source is the key to the entire problem.
This action might well be taken under a progressive program of education as was listed in the magna carta put forward by Mr. Robi-chaud, the former minister of fisheries, in his proposals for the entire industry.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Another factor adding to the low returns received by the freshwater fishermen is the fact that fresh fish spoils quickly unless properly iced or refrigerated. In view of the distance between our major exporters and the importers in New York, Chicago, and Detroit, and the absence of effective quality control in Canada, our exporters are frequently faced

with claims of poor quality, with no assurance that such deterioration has in fact taken place and, if it did, whether it occurred prior to arrival or resulted from mismanagement at the hands of the importer. This applies to fish exported in the whole round or in dressed form; but generally speaking it does not apply to fish fillets. At present over 95 per cent of all freshwater fish exports or three quarters of our total Canadian production is exported to the United States. In fact, we are the only foreign supplier in that market and U.S. importers depend on Canadian production for nearly all their requirements of pickerel, pike, sauger, whitefish and lake trout. However, in Chicago and Detroit two out of nine importers handle most of the Canadian shipments from some 35 exporters, which makes these two importers the dominant controllers in the pricing of round or dressed freshwater fish.
After making a study of the freshwater fishing industry and comparing it with the saltwater fishing industry as I know it, I can only conclude that the freshwater fishing industry has not progressed very far from the days of Peter, the great fisherman of Bible days. The supermarkets are today the great retailers for the fishing industry. Canadian exporters generally encounter fewer problems and have a stronger bargaining position when marketing fillets than when selling dressed fish; and today's modern housewife has indicated she prefers fillets to fish in the round or dressed state. Exporters can sell fillets, not to an importer distributor, but direct to a retail chain or large outlet. Since there are a large number of importers of fillets, control over the export of fish in this form is not nearly as concentrated as for round or dressed fish. I would therefore suggest that the government give greater consideration to the services provided to our freshwater fishermen by our exporters and dealers before they concur with the recommendations of the provinces which grant licences to some 93 exporters in our freshwater fishery areas. Exporters and dealers should be requested to upgrade their storage facilities and filleting equipment; and with closer quality control our freshwater fishermen could enjoy a better price for their product.
To ensure that our freshwater fishermen are better informed of the prices paid for their product in our major United States markets, I would also suggest that the federal government use the facilities of the C.B.C. to broadcast a daily fisherman's log through the
December 18. 1968

Fisheries
network of stations covering our inland fishing areas. This would be helpful in keeping dealers and fishermen on their toes and would help to bring about some uniformity of prices paid to our freshwater fishermen who must of necessity carry out their operations in areas separated by vast distances.
There are many other matters I wish to raise which might be helpful to our freshwater fishermen, but I will not do so, since I believe my time is running short. I look at this resolution with mixed feelings. It seems to be a direct contradiction of the fisheries minister's statement made in Boston on October 18, 1968, when he said this:
I believe in free enterprise, and I believe in the free interplay of supply and demand. I believe that competition is an important discipline in our economic system. And I believe that competition is, itself, the best assurance that the consumer at the market end of the line will get his fish at the lowest possible price. Having said that I must be quick to point out that there are too many obstacles to free enterprise, to free trade, and to the effective marketing of our fishery products. These barriers should be torn down so that all these forces should be free to work for the common good.
I ask the minister of Fisheries what has happened to these high sounding ideals? I am sorry to see that he is not in his seat this afternoon. I realize of course that he may be absent trying to solve some of the problems of our fishing industry at the present time. I ask why he does not assist the fishermen and the freshwater fishing industry in the modernization of its plants and equipment, as promised by his predecessor? Or for that matter, why does he not use the Fisheries Prices Support Act to beef up the prices of those fish which are producing incomes below the poverty line so that "economic encouragement is adopted", as promised by Mr. Robi-chaud? He also promised improved credit facilities for our fishermen; and this promise, if implemented, would help our freshwater fishermen to get boats and equipment so that they would not be dependant on the fish merchants.
Why has no action been taken by the government on order No. 9, the measure to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, which would help our inland fishermen obtain boats and equipment? This has been on the order paper since parliament opened. With an apparent lack of understanding of our problems on the part of the government no action has been taken on this very vital and necessary piece of legislation. New research programs would help our freshwater fisherman to properly ice and improve the quality of his
product. Exploration programs may also clean up some of the pollution of our rivers and lakes which has cut the earnings of our Great Lakes fishermen in half. And technical training could help all our fishermen, both inland and on the coast, in faster and easier methods of catching fish. The promises have been made to our fishermen. They were made to them in 1964 and it is time we saw some action.
I said I looked at this resolution with mixed feelings. I do so because it leaves many questions unanswered. For example, who will appoint the representatives of this corporation; will they be appointed by the federal or by the provincial governments concerned? How many will there be, and how great a load will their salaries and expenses be on the backs of the average freshwater fishermen? How many provinces and areas will be covered? Does the resolution cover the entire great lakes area with its large perch, smelt, bass and cisco landings? If it does not cover the southern part of the great lakes area, including lake Erie, and the marketing corporation principle is sound, why was this area excluded? What effect will this have on our fisheries sales in the U.S. which refused to lower the tariff on yellow perch when it was supported last year by the Fisheries Prices Support Board, at a loss of $523,535.13? If this had been the freshwater fish marketing corporation, who would make up the loss, the government or the fishermen? How are the prices under this corporation to be determined? Who sets the market? Who is the government guesser? What will happen to the plants made redundant by this legislation?
The minister said, as reported at page 3465 of Hansard for December 3:
The corporation would not be Intended to duplicate existing facilities of the industry. It should seek to reduce unnecessary duplication of facilities

Those are his words.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will keep my comments on this resolution very brief. Our party welcomes this resolution. We are not devoted or doctrinaire adherents of free enterprise-to echo an expression which I think the minister used on December 3. I think this particular form of free enterprise has left many fishermen in destitution and we are all in favour of seeing the corporation set up without delay, in order that it may help in the marketing of the products of the fishermen.
I must confess that I find myself slightly surprised to be discussing the subject of fisheries. I do not pose as an expert, though I am an appreciative consumer. My own constituency of Greenwood in Toronto is an urban constituency and not noted as a fishing centre. Yet it happens to be a fact that in our area there is a prospective fishing industry. We are right on top of a very large body of fresh water, lake Ontario, and I am given to understand that there is a real opportunity to develop a fishing industry through the use of modern methods and modern trawlers, particularly with respect to a fish named shad- and I hope no one will ask me what shad is. I think they have other, more picturesque names for it than shad. But I am told by some of my constituents that there is a very real opportunity for development in this field. This is what makes me ask the question. The hon. member for South Shore asked why, in view of previous promises made, this legislation applied only to freshwater fisheries. I ask, why is it so regionally restricted? I notice that the acting minister when speaking on December 3 said the bill will enable the establishment of board marketing of freshwater fish produced in the prairie provinces, the Northwest Territories and northwestern Ontario.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The resolution itself is not so geographically restricted. I want to know why freshwater

fisheries-and there are some-in other sections of the internal waterways of Canada are to be excluded from the benefits of this legislation, if indeed that is the intention. I do not begrudge the benefits of the legislation to people in the prairie provinces, the Northwest Territories and northwestern Ontario. There may be an urgent need there. But why should the legislation be restricted, if indeed this is the case, to these particular geographical areas? I presume that if northern Ontario is to be included, Ontario will be one of the provinces co-operating in the setting up of the corporation. But I still do not understand this limitation and would like to know the reason for it.
I will conclude my remarks by saying we welcome this resolution because it seems to us, without having seen the details of the bill, that it represents a very healthy approach to some of the problems of people who are living under conditions of extreme poverty in this country. It envisages co-operation among the producers, the provincial governments on one side and the federal government on the other. Any illustration of this sort of co-operation among producers and governments both provincial and federal to raise the standards of our people is something that meets with our approval.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in commenting on the resolution for the introduction of a bill to establish a freshwater fish board with powers to buy fish direct from the fishermen and sell to the ultimate consumer, mainly in the United States, I would say that the bill is the result of the Mclvor commission report of 1966, which has since created throughout the industry indecision, indirection and a lack of purpose to the extent that the industry is languishing because almost no capital has been invested in it. This is the situation as far as the processing and transportation of freshwater fish is concerned. Therefore this bill is welcomed because it will put an end to the indecision that for the last three years has plagued the industry.
The fishing industry in my riding borders lakes Winnipegosis and Manitoba. It has provided almost half of Manitoba's freshwater fish. The industry has been active for over 70 years and has provided a livelihood, although a dwindling one, for a number of citizens in that time. Unfortunately, during this time there has been little improvement in the methods of fishing and little upgrading in the output per man-hour. It seems to me that the industry, being small and the fishermen
December 18. 1968

individuals who often operate part time, does not lend itself to large capital investment that would improve the output of high quality fish. Indeed, I am told that other than the introduction of nylon mesh nets there has in the past 40 years been little change in the fishing on lakes Winnipegosis and Manitoba.
The fishermen involved vary from families who over the years have found the industry has provided them with an occupation giving a reasonable standard of living, down to many marginal people who eke out a living on a part time basis. One survey indicates that over half the fishermen are Indians, with many more Metis people, so that in many respects this board could be considered to be a development board with the idea of helping these people to either achieve a better standard of living with increased income or phase out their operations and disperse the fishermen into more gainful occupations which will provide a better income.
Approximately 80 per cent of the fish is sold on international markets, mainly in Chicago, Cleveland and New York. Although the minister has implied that the freshwater fish industry has an almost captive market, it comes into competition with saltwater fish, meats and other animal protein foods, so there is a definite limit to what this product will bring in markets related to other meats. In other words, the price is dependant on the price of other consumer meats in the great American cities where freshwater fish is marketed.
One of the great problems of the industry has been the failure to supply a uniform product to the consumer and the inspection and grading of fish has been inadequate, resulting in wide variations in quality. This has detracted from the saleability of the fish. In this area the government, either provincial or federal, which alone can supply adequate inspection facilities, seems to have been derelict in its duty.
The fish products have been bought by fish companies, which in turn have exported the fish to the United States markets. The fish companies need export licences which are obtainable from the province in which they operate. My understanding is that over half the fish the marketing of which will be affected by this bill comes from Winnipeg. These companies vary a great deal in size, facilities and ability to market fish in the continental U.S. markets. Some companies in Winnipeg- these are limited to four or five-seem to have adequate storage, marketing, processing
Fisheries
and transportation facilities and have been able to advance to the fishermen a reasonable amount of money as an initial payment. However, there are other companies with very limited facilities to process, store and export fish and there has been complaint that such companies may operate to drive down the price of fish to the producer. It is hoped that this board will provide a more orderly marketing in the freshwater fish industry.
There has been widespread feeling among fishermen that the fish companies have taken advantage of the economic position of the fisherman and his vulnerability to changes in price and supply, and have made considerable profits at the expense of the fishermen. The fish companies' reply to this complaint is that their profits have not been large and that an examination of their books would not indicate that theirs has been a very lucrative business. Another complaint is that the fish companies have not made any great effort to expand marketing facilities or invest further in processing and storage. The implementation of this bill will at least settle that problem, whether it be that the fish companies should expand further or be taken over by the government.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
One of the problems, of course, is that the fish caught are of two main varieties. There are those of the marketable variety bringing a fairly good price on the market, and large quantities of so-called coarse fish that have a very low saleability. Various uses of this coarse fish have been investigated, such as use in conjunction with alfalfa plants etc., but the answer from the processors is that it is quite an expensive method of providing protein, even at the low price which the fish bring to the producer. However, these coarse fish must be removed, along with the saleable varieties, otherwise the lakes would soon produce no fish at all, so in some aspects fishing is necessary in order to keep the good species available. One of the most promising aspects of the statement of the minister is that research will be carried on to attempt to make the lakes more productive, and I feel that in the long run this is an approach that might well make the industry reasonably productive and provide for its people a reasonable level of income.
I should like to point out that marketing boards in the past have been less than successful in many fields. Most marketing boards that have been successful have dealt

December 18, 1963
Fisheries
with commodities such as grain, that is nonperishable, which have relatively few importers or exporters and which can be stored for long periods of time.
Even producer boards which operate in the interest of producers alone have not always fared too well. When there is a marketing problem, the reference of the marketing to a board does not automatically ease the problem or cure it. The seasonal nature of the freshwater fish industry, the low level of the productivity of many of the fishermen, the scattered nature of the various sources of fish, scattered over hundreds of thousands of square miles, and the fact that the fishing industry as a whole is in a serious state, as we well know from listening to the maritime members in this house, coupled with the fact that many of the freshwater fishermen are at a sustenance level, will make the work of this board difficult for some time. The hope is expressed that this board can bring about rationalization, price stability and marketing quality.
I will await this bill with considerable interest to see what ideas the government may have on bringing a reasonable degree of stability to this industry. However, I will withhold my judgment whether or not his marketing board will be successful in raising the level of income of the fishermen who are mainly living at a sustenance level,

Mr. Chairman, I think it is in order, in beginning my few remarks on this resolution, to refer to the fact, which is perhaps more important than the resolution itself, that we do not have with us today either the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce or the minister to whom I and my colleagues have posed questions day after day concerning the marketing of fish, namely the Minister of Fisheries or his parliamentary secretary. This perhaps in itself is indicative of an attitude which has pervaded the nation regarding the fishing industry of Canada. We have been asking questions day after day regarding the government's position on fisheries, its policy and its programs. We have had nothing more than shrugs of shoulders and frivolous remarks here and there, a sort of comic relief for the house, when the problem of fisheries is brought before the house for discussion. I think the absence today of the ministers concerned and of other members who should be taking an active interest in fisheries should be brought to the attention of the house because one of the saddest things about our fishing industry is that no one in

the Liberal government seems to care very much any longer about what is going on.
In 1963, amazingly enough, the Pearson government during its election campaign made a great statement that the government, if elected, would bring before the house and put before the nation a great program to solve the problems of our fishing industry. Of course, true to the words of the man who became prime minister after the 1963 election, a meeting of the provincial ministers of fisheries was held in 1964 at which a statement was made, which was quoted today by the hon. member for South Shore, that the federal government was going to bring forward a Magna Carta for the fishing industry of Canada. This statement was made by the former minister of fisheries, Mr. Robichaud.
In considering the resolution before the house today we are reminded of the words of the President of the Privy Council spoken on December 3, 1968 as recorded at page 3464 of Hansard. This is what he said:
I might remind hon. members, Mr. Chairman, that in 1964 a federal-provincial conference established a committee to study this whole question. After this study was made, in 1965 the Mclvor commission was appointed to look into the question. The commission agreed largely with the findings of the province of Manitoba, which had also studied the matter and in which province aproximately 40 per cent of the production originates.
I can only conclude that what we are studying here now is the magna carta for the fishing industry of the Canadian nation. Day after day since the house opened in September we have posed questions regarding the government's policy on fisheries. We asked what the government's position was regarding the whole fishing industry of Canada.

I agree with the hon. member that they had no policy. Back in September some of my colleagues asked questions of the Minister of Fisheries who answered that the government was going to make an announcement very shortly on the fishing industry of Canada and on its policy. We have received the same answer day after day. Meanwhile, the industry has gone on the rocks, and now we are faced with a resolution which was brought in the first day the house opened and which is presented to the house for debate only today. I wonder why it has taken so long to come before the house, and yet we are to believe that this is the magna carta for the fishing industry. My great regret is that some of my colleagues
December 18, 1968

who have a great knowledge of the fishing industry were not given the opportunity during the past election-but perhaps they will have it in the next election-to bring their influence to bear in solving many of our problems.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to a remark which was made with regard to the resolution. May I say that if the goals of this resolution are ever to be reached, then nobody can take exception to it. Of course the ideals were enunciated at page 3464 of Hansard, as follows:
The objectives of this legislation will be a more orderly marketing for the benefit of the whole fishery, and by this means the achievement of higher and more stable prices for the catch; to provide the fishermen with a better share of the market value of their fish; and to expand total sales and over-all production in the fishery.
These ideals, as enunciated in the house on December 3, cannot be taken exception to. I think it is commendable of the government to have such an attitude, but I wonder if this answers all the problems faced by the Canadian fishery. I contend that there is a great contradiction between this statement on the goals of the resolution and a statement contained in the resolution which states that the purpose of the marketing board is:
-to provide that the corporation shall conduct its operations on a self-sustaining financial basis without appropriations therefor by parliament;
Might I stress the fact that the marketing board is to conduct its operations on a selfsustaining financial basis. I think it is a very important statement.
There is another point which concerns me-and I regret, as I am sure do all hon. members, that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Fisheries are not here to speak on that point.
I wonder if it is true that the government has given up its interest in the Canadian fishing industry, which appears to be the case. I am not sure whether this is a result of the government's lack of interest, or of some pressure being put on it from the outside. For example, 1 remember asking the Minister of Fisheries a question during a committee hearing about two weeks ago to which he replied that a commitment had been made to the United States government that the deficiency payments to the fishing industry would be discontinued at the end of October. There was a further commitment that the government of Canada would not involve itself in any form of assistance to the industry that may be construed as aid or as a subsidy. I am wondering
Fisheries
if this is the reason for the inclusion of this definite indication that the industry has to pay its way. I would be delighted if this government could introduce a program indicating the government's desire to put the industry on its legs. Then, if the industry shows it can be self-sustaining we will be satisfied, but that provision should be made before the industry is asked to be self-sustaining. The minister made a similar statement in Boston, and it is included here. He said we were setting up a corporation to help the industry. The first thing the government says, however, is that the industry had better pay its way because the government is not going to give it any assistance.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The minister admits the United States government has not taken issue with this attitude. The U.S. government stated they were going to go along with the commitment that no help would be given the industry, regardless of the situation in which this already disabled industry finds itself. Again we have to look back upon what has happened in the past few months. The federal government was paying the Atlantic fishermen a little assistance on the salt they used for the preservation of their catch. This amounted to $300,000, almost as much as will be spent on the great festivities connected with the opening of the cultural centre in Ottawa. This was the amount of money being paid by the Canadian government to Atlantic fishermen. It was taken away at the beginning of this year. Then we lost the insurance which was being paid for the fishermen. This insurance was taken away on the flimsy excuse that not many people claimed losses, so it did not serve any purpose.
The deficiency payments were cut off as of October 30. These things indicate the way this government has literally given up the ghost on this industry and allowed it to go by the boards. If this is the answer with which the government of Canada is coming up for our fishing industry for the whole country, then I say we are in an extremely sad state of affairs. We are all aware of the many problems the industry faces. Only last Friday evening my colleagues in this party had a chance to present to the Minister of Fisheries the serious state of affairs- facing the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast. I am not sure that we convinced him how serious the situation was. This week there was the announcement of a very tragic situation. I think perhaps some hon. members might not agree

December 18. 1968
Fisheries
with this, but one of our biggest fishing industries announced that it was closing. We have lost four fish plants and we will lose another ten on the east coast in another week or so. Four thousand people are out of work right at the moment.
My colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East, as well as other members, rose in the house on the day the announcement was made, to question the Prime Minister. He shrugged his shoulders and said he was unable to pull the answers out of his hip pocket. His ministers were not in the house. We did not get any chance to ask the Minister of Fisheries any questions, nor did we get any satisfactory answers. I am afraid the whole economy of one of our provinces will go by the boards unless the government listens to representations from the Atlantic area. I am sure some members in the house have wondered if the situation were really serious, but I am sure they realize now the serious condition of the industry.
We have a prices support board which came into existence a number of years ago. There was a review of that program and the board was reinstituted in 1952. This prices support board gives the government all the power it needs to take care of the slump in our industry. The government has done nothing. The industry is going on the rocks and we sit by. We are going to wait until tomorrow or next week, but still nothing worth while comes from the government. I am wondering if the government has the intention of trying to beef up the industry, or if it is going to sit by and allow it to go on the rocks. If we do not get action of a general nature in a matter of weeks, we won't have to worry. As I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity said last week, we will not have to solve the problems of the fishing industry but instead we will have the problem of creating a fishing industry, since there will be nothing left.
I am not going to continue any longer. I believe some concepts in the resolution are healthy. I think the expansion of this idea in some directions might be healthy, too. All I am saying is that it grieves me to stand here in the house, having taken up fisheries problems in Canada since 1964, and have to accept this as the Magna Carta of the fishing industry. If this is the Magna Carta of the fishing industry, then God help it.

We had a manifestation of the same arrogance a few months ago when the minister cancelled the salt rebate program. Granted, this was an ad hoc program, but the minister cancelled it right in the middle of the fishing season. The obvious question to ask is: Why not wait until the end of the season? subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION
speechtext:
It will be less after this, because it will be nil. These fishermen still have to buy food and pay the same prices paid by people much better endowed. They still have to buy their gear. What is even worse, they have to suffer under a government that does not seem to care about them. "Let them eat cake" is the attitude of the government. Let more plants close down.
The minister admitted that there were a few efficient plants in the maritimes and that he still has great hopes for the industry and that it will become more efficient. Then he said that the government will come up with a program in its own good time. As a matter of fact, he said, if I may paraphrase him: We plan on coming in with a new program in March of next year.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat referred to the Magna Carta of the last government, which was in January, 1964. According to the Ottawa Journal for January 25, 1964, Hon. H. J. Robichaud announced a Magna Carta for fishermen. The fishermen were to be placed on a par with the farmers of Canada. If I may just read part of this article, it commences:
Winding up five days of closed talks, the federal-provincial fisheries conference came forth Friday with a pledge to design a national development program that would bring Canadian fishermen the same benefits given to farmers.
In 1964 the same government was in power that is in power today. We have a new Minister of Fisheries from the province of British Columbia, of which he boasted last night when saying some disparaging things about the province of Newfoundland, to the effect that we can only suffer by comparison. But still there is no fisheries policy in this country. Where is the Magna Carta of 1964, so much talked of and so much heralded, in the program of the government today? Even the premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Smallwood, was ecstatic about the conference results. According to the article he said there was agreement on all sides for the proposition that the fishing industry should be treated the same as agriculture, and he called it a Magna Carta for the fishing industry.

December 18/ 1968
Fisheries
Today we see seven fish plants having to close down, or in the process of closing down, and the minister announcing on television last night that there will have to be further shutdowns if the industry is to become more efficient. I have one question for the Minister of Fisheries, and I am sorry that he is not here now. What is to become of the Canadian citizens who eke out a living working 50 or 60 hours a week in fish plants and consider themselves blessed to have the opportunity to do so? What will become of them if there are further shutdowns in the industry?
In the Atlantic provinces today this government stands condemned as being without heart, cold and calculating. One can only compare its policy to what happened in Russia in the 1930's.

speechtext:
The hon. member says "six o'clock". It looks as though it is the eleventh hour for the fishing industry because it is on the verge of total collapse.
I have one further comment to make. If the government does not realize the seriousness of the situation and what is involved in human terms here, then we will have a crisis in this country that will be unprecedented in its proportions.
Before I resume my seat may I say we are anxious to see the legislation. The freshwater fish industry will be affected by the legislation, and the provincial governments are both involved and anxious to see this bill, as are all of us. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we have no objection to the resolution passing at this time.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, might we fail to see the clock for a moment and with the consent of the committee, if no other hon. members wish to speak, carry the resolution and see the bill?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION
speechtext: We on this side are agreed to that, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I think many of the questions asked by hon. members opposite will be answered, or certainly sharpened, by the bill itself, and I look forward to their having the chance to see it. The bill has resulted from many discussions between the provincial governments and the federal government, and of course the report of the Mclvor commission.
One hon. member asked whether this was a matter in which the provincial governments
had co-operated or were willing to accept. It is indeed something that they want very badly indeed. I may say to the hon. member for Greenwood that the question as to which areas are included under the bill depends largely upon discussions and the indications of interest by the provinces in regard to what can be worked out at this time. This bill and all the discussions connected therewith have had the very close attention of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as well as the Minister of Fisheries, who unfortunately cannot be here at the moment because both are on urgent government business. I was joining them when I was suddenly and somewhat unexpectedly summoned to deal with this matter.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I thank hon. members for their patience.
I should like to express appreciation to the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley and to the hon. member for the Northwest Territories for agreeing to reserve their comments until second reading. I may say I have also discussed this matter with the hon. member for Essex, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries, who is keenly interested in this subject.
A board of the kind proposed could do a great deal to meet the marketing problems of this industry, and the difficulties surrounding its rationalization. It could help to deal with the situation which arises when a number of suppliers are suddenly able to enter the market. I look forward to further debate on the bill and on that occasion I shall try to deal with the sharpened questions asked by hon. members.
